research.how_top_tier_does_it:
## 1. The local database is the application, the network is a replication detail

**Signal-Android (DOCUMENTED, source code).** Sending a message is not a network call. `MessageSender` writes a row into the local SQLite `messages` table first, then enqueues a persisted job. `IndividualSendJob` is constructed with `Job.Parameters` that carry the whole reliability policy declaratively:
- `queue = recipient.id.toQueueKey(hasMedia)` — a *per-recipient* serial queue. Two messages to the same person can never race or reorder; two messages to different people run in parallel. Scheduled sends get a separate `toScheduledSendQueueKey()`.
- `constraints = [NetworkConstraint.KEY, SealedSenderConstraint.KEY]` — the job is not attempted at all until the OS reports a network. There is no "try and fail" burn on airplane mode.
- `lifespan = TimeUnit.DAYS.toMillis(1)` (86,400,000 ms), `maxAttempts = Parameters.UNLIMITED`. Retry forever, but only for 24 hours.
- `onFailure()` → `SignalDatabase.messages.markAsSentFailed(messageId)` + `notifyMediaMessageDeliveryFailed(...)`. Terminal failure is a **state transition in the local DB**, which the UI is already bound to. Nothing is swallowed and nothing needs a live listener to observe it.
(https://github.com/signalapp/Signal-Android/blob/main/app/src/main/java/org/thoughtcrime/securesms/jobs/IndividualSendJob.kt)

Defaults in `Job.java` are deliberately hostile: `maxAttempts = 1`, `lifespan = IMMORTAL (-1)`, plus explicit priority tiers (`PRIORITY_HIGH=1`, `DEFAULT=0`, `LOW=-1`, `LOWER=-2`). Every job has to opt into retry, so nothing retries by accident. The jobmanager package persists jobs (`persistence/`, `JsonJobData`), migrates them across app versions (`JobMigrator`), reschedules after reboot (`BootReceiver`), and drives execution from `AlarmManagerScheduler` + `JobSchedulerScheduler` via `CompositeScheduler`. The queue survives process death, app upgrade, and reboot.

Backoff (DOCUMENTED, `BackoffUtil.java`): `2^min(attempt,30) * 1000 ms`, clamped by `Math.min(exponentialBackoff, maxBackoff)` where maxBackoff is remote-config'd (was 30 s), then multiplied by a jitter factor `0.75 + random()*0.5` (±25%). Note this is *proportional* jitter, weaker than AWS "Full Jitter", but it is enough because Signal's contention is a few thousand clients hitting one endpoint after an outage, not N clients CAS-looping one row.

**Telegram / TDLib (DOCUMENTED).** The client persists a durable replication state `{pts, qts, date, seq}` plus a per-channel `pts`. Every update carries the sequence position it advances to and how many events it covers (`pts_count`). The client validates locally: if `local_seq + 1 == seq_start`, apply; if `local_seq + 1 > seq_start`, it is a redelivery — **discard, idempotently**; if `local_seq + 1 < seq_start` there is a hole, so buffer and call `updates.getDifference` / `updates.getChannelDifference` to fill it. Gaps are *impossible to miss* because they are detected arithmetically, not by hoping the socket stayed up. TDLib is explicitly described as owning "networking, local storage and data consistency". Known limits: `getDifference` results do not themselves carry sequences (the client must trust the server for that batch), and `ChannelDifferenceTooLong` is unrecoverable — the client throws that channel away and resyncs it from scratch.
(https://core.telegram.org/api/updates, https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/gotd/td/telegram/updates)

**WhatsApp (DOCUMENTED, whitepaper).** For multi-device app state (chat mutes, archives, contacts), the server holds a **Patch Queue** per collection; each patch has a monotonic version and a client-computed `PatchMAC`. A server-side "Base Roller" periodically compacts the queue into a **Snapshot** with a `SnapshotMAC`. The integrity primitive is `LtHash16`, a 1024-bit **homomorphic** set hash: because it is homomorphic, a client can take the hash of the old snapshot, add/subtract the deltas from the patches it just applied, and get a value that must equal the server's declared snapshot hash — so a client that has been offline for a month can accept a compacted snapshot it never watched being built and still prove the server did not tamper with or drop any mutation. Catch-up is "give me patches after version V", falling back to snapshot+patches when V is too old — structurally identical to Telegram's `getDifference` / `differenceTooLong`.
(https://www.whatsapp.com/security/WhatsApp-Security-Whitepaper.pdf)

**Linear (DOCUMENTED via reverse-engineering repo endorsed by Linear's CTO).** `lastSyncId` is a single global monotonically-incrementing integer — the version number of the whole database. Server mutations increment it and are broadcast as **delta packets** (typed sync actions: Insert / Update / Archive / Delete / Covering / sync-group changes) carrying full changed property values, not just acks. On WebSocket reconnect the handshake compares the client's `lastSyncId` against the server's; any shortfall is a request for the missing delta range. Client writes live in a transaction queue with four explicit phases — `createdTransactions`, `queuedTransactions`, `executingTransactions`, `persistedTransactionsEnqueue` — and are **serialized into an IndexedDB `__transactions` table before being sent**, so a crash mid-flight replays on next launch. Transactions created in the same event-loop turn share a `batchIndex` and are flushed together by a microtask scheduler, bounded by a mutation-size limit. Conflict policy is last-writer-wins with rebasing: when a delta packet lands for a property with a still-executing local transaction, the transaction's base value is updated to the server value and the in-memory model is re-pointed at the pending local value (OT-like behaviour without transformation functions).
(https://github.com/wzhudev/reverse-linear-sync-engine)

**Figma (DOCUMENTED).** Explicitly rejected both OT ("a combinatorial explosion of possible states") and CRDTs (designed for decentralised systems; with an authoritative server "we can simplify our system by removing this extra overhead"). The model is a **last-writer-wins register per object-property**, with the server defining the total order — no vector clocks, no timestamps. The client-side anti-flicker rule is the important one: *the client discards incoming server changes that conflict with its own unacknowledged property changes*, because the unacked local value is "our best prediction of what the eventually-consistent value will be". Offline reconnect after an arbitrary gap: download a fresh document, reapply local offline edits on top, resume streaming.
(https://www.figma.com/blog/how-figmas-multiplayer-technology-works/)

**PowerSync (DOCUMENTED)** is the closest thing to a productised version of this for Postgres. Server-side data is partitioned into **sync buckets** (parameterised, e.g. `user_todo_lists["A"]`), each an ordered op-log of PUT/REMOVE with monotonic op ids. A row is only deleted client-side when removed from *all* buckets containing it. Sync rounds are **checkpoints**: client sends its per-bucket last op id, server replies with a checkpoint id + per-bucket checksums, streams ops, then signals checkpoint complete — so the client only makes data visible at a consistent boundary, never mid-stream. Checksum mismatch → delete the bucket and re-sync it (same escape hatch as `ChannelDifferenceTooLong`). Local writes go to an **upload queue**; after uploading, the client requests a **write checkpoint**, and the server confirms durability by tracking the CDC position (Postgres LSN) — so "my write is safely replicated" is a positive, provable signal rather than a 200 OK.
(https://docs.powersync.com/architecture/powersync-protocol)

## 2. The composite pattern all five share

1. **Client-generated stable id** on the write (UUID). It is the idempotency key for retries and the dedupe key for the server echo.
2. **Single atomic local transaction**: write the entity row *and* the outbox row together. Never write the entity and then "remember to enqueue".
3. **Optimistic apply to the read model immediately**, with an explicit `sending / sent / failed` status column — not a separate in-memory list.
4. **A worker drains the outbox** under a network constraint, serialised per logical stream, with exponential backoff + jitter and a lifespan cap.
5. **The server assigns the authoritative order** (`seq` / `pts` / `lastSyncId` / op id). Clients never invent ordering.
6. **A persisted cursor** advances *only after the local apply commits*. Cursor-then-apply is the classic data-loss bug.
7. **Reconnect is not "resubscribe"** — it is "compare cursor, fetch the difference, then resubscribe", with a hard fallback to full resync when the gap is too old.
8. **Terminal failure is a persisted state**, rendered in the row itself, with a retry affordance.

## 3. Retry, backoff, coalescing, and the train

**Backoff (DOCUMENTED, AWS).** Exact formulas:
- no jitter: `sleep = min(cap, base * 2^attempt)`
- **Full Jitter**: `sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))`
- Equal Jitter: `sleep = min(cap, base*2^attempt)/2 + random(0, min(cap, base*2^attempt)/2)`
- Decorrelated Jitter: `sleep = min(cap, random(base, sleep*3))`

Simulated with 100 contending clients over a 10 ms-mean / 4 ms-variance network: Full and Equal Jitter each cut total calls by **more than half** vs. un-jittered backoff. Full Jitter does the least work (slightly more wall-clock); Equal Jitter does more work *and* takes much longer; Decorrelated does slightly more work than Full. **Full Jitter is the default choice.** The post is explicit that jitter does not change the underlying O(N²) contention — it only stops synchronised retry storms.
(https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/)

**Request coalescing (singleflight).** Key in-flight operations by a stable key; a second caller for the same key attaches to the existing future instead of issuing a second request. Critical caveat: singleflight is per-process — it deduplicates within one client, it does not deduplicate across the fleet. On the client the keys that matter are "fetch messages since cursor X for conversation C" and "refresh session", both of which get hammered on every resume/reconnect.

**Connectivity is a hint, never a gate (DOCUMENTED).** `connectivity_plus`' own README: "Connection type availability does not guarantee that there is an Internet access... You should not rely on the current connectivity status to decide whether you can reliably make a network request." Android's `NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET` means the network claims internet; `NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED` means the OS actually probed successfully — you need both, and even then a captive portal or a dying cell handoff will still fail. Correct shape: use connectivity events to *wake the drainer early* and to reset backoff, but let the actual request timeout be the authority.

**Train behaviour (30 s tunnels, repeated).** The failure that hurts is not the outage, it is the **reconnect stampede** afterwards: socket reconnect + token refresh + catch-up fetch + image reloads all firing at once, on the worst 200 ms of signal, from every user in the carriage simultaneously. What good clients do:
- Never block the UI thread or the user's action on the network; the local write already succeeded.
- Backoff resets to base on a *successful* request, not on a connectivity event — otherwise every tunnel exit resets everyone to zero simultaneously (this is precisely the correlated-retry case jitter exists for).
- Coalesce the resume storm: one catch-up request per conversation keyed by cursor, hedged behind a short debounce (a few hundred ms) so `onResume` + `connectivity change` + `socket open` produce one fetch, not three.
- Treat "socket open" as unproven: the first thing after reconnect is the cursor comparison, and until it completes the UI shows the local data, not a spinner.
- Push is the backstop, not the transport. FCM stores and retries for **up to 2,419,200 s (28 days)**, default four weeks; **max 4 distinct active collapse keys** per token; **max 100 pending messages** stored per app instance for a disconnected device (after that FCM discards and sends a `deleted_messages` tickle — the client's answer to that must be "run the cursor catch-up", which is exactly why the cursor must be persisted). High-priority messages can wake a device in Doze with limited network access; FCM uses **7 days** of behavioural history to decide whether to deprioritise a sender that does not produce user-visible notifications.
(https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud-messaging/customize-messages/setting-message-lifespan, https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud-messaging/android/message-priority)

## 4. Flutter: the frame budget and where it goes

**Budget (DOCUMENTED).** 60 fps ⇒ **~16 ms per frame**; the docs split it as roughly **8 ms UI thread + 8 ms raster thread**. 120 Hz devices ⇒ **under 8 ms total**. The performance overlay shows the **last 300 frames** for UI and raster separately; **white lines mark 16 ms increments**; red bars mark over-budget frames. Red on the UI graph = your Dart is too expensive; red on the raster graph = the scene is too expensive to draw.
(https://docs.flutter.dev/perf/ui-performance)

**The expensive things, in order (DOCUMENTED).**
- `saveLayer()` — allocates an offscreen buffer and forces a render-target switch, "particularly disruptive on mobile GPUs". Triggered by `ShaderMask`, `ColorFilter`, `Chip` with `disabledColorAlpha != 0xff`, `Text` with an `overflowShader`, and `Clip.antiAliasWithSaveLayer`. Detect with `checkerboardOffscreenLayers`.
- `Opacity` in animations — use `AnimatedOpacity` / `FadeInImage`, or bake the alpha into the colour when there is no overlap.
- Clipping — cheaper than `saveLayer` but still real; prefer `borderRadius` over a clip; pre-clip before animating.
- **Intrinsic passes** — two layout passes instead of one, and they poll *all* cells of a grid/list rather than the visible ones. Enable "Track layouts" in DevTools and look for `'$runtimeType intrinsics'` events. Fix by fixing cell size or nominating an anchor cell.
- `AnimatedBuilder.builder` containing subtrees that do not depend on the animation — those rebuild every tick. Hoist them into the `child` parameter.
- Overriding `operator ==` on widgets → **O(N²)** behaviour.
- Non-lazy `Column`/`ListView(children: [...])` for mostly-offscreen content.

**List virtualisation (DOCUMENTED).** `ListView.builder`/`.separated`/`.custom` build lazily; the default constructor builds everything. `RenderAbstractViewport.defaultCacheExtent = 250.0` **logical pixels** of off-screen build-ahead on each side — so a list of ~90 px rows keeps ~3 extra rows live per edge; a list of full-screen items keeps a fraction of one. `itemExtent` or `prototypeItem` is documented as "more efficient than letting the children determine their own extent because the scrolling machinery can make use of the foreknowledge". `addAutomaticKeepAlives` and `addRepaintBoundaries` both default to `true`.
(https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/widgets/ListView-class.html, https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/rendering/RenderAbstractViewport/defaultCacheExtent-constant.html)

**Images (DOCUMENTED).** `ImageCache` defaults: **1000 images and 100 MB**, LRU, with three populations — pending, cached (keepAlive), and *live* (has listeners, count never dropped to zero). `clear()` does not touch live images; `clearLiveImages()` does. `ResizeImage` "instructs Flutter to decode the image at the specified dimensions instead of at its native size" and is "generally used to reduce the memory footprint of ImageCache" — `Image.network(..., cacheWidth:)` composes it via `ResizeImage.resizeIfNeeded`. The decode cost and the cache cost are both a function of the *decoded* pixel count, so a 4000×3000 JPEG costs ~48 MB of RGBA regardless of the 220 dp box you draw it in; `cacheWidth` at device-pixel size cuts that by ~2 orders of magnitude.
(https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/painting/ImageCache-class.html, https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/painting/ResizeImage-class.html)

**Isolates (DOCUMENTED).** "Use isolates when large computations cause UI jank" — i.e. anything that can exceed the frame gap. `Isolate.run(callback)` for one-shot; on mobile `await compute(fn, msg)` ≡ `await Isolate.run(() => fn(msg))`. Messages are **copied**, except immutable objects (Strings, unmodifiable byte buffers) which pass by reference, and `Isolate.exit` which transfers ownership without copying. There is real overhead in both spawning and copying, so repeated work should use a **long-lived** isolate (`Isolate.spawn` + `ReceivePort`/`SendPort`). Background isolates cannot access `rootBundle`/`dart:ui` and cannot receive unsolicited platform-channel messages — you can *query* from an isolate but you cannot host a long-lived platform listener there.
(https://docs.flutter.dev/perf/isolates)

**Impeller (DOCUMENTED).** Default since **Flutter 3.27** on iOS and **Android API 29+**; below API 29 or without a working Vulkan driver it falls back to OpenGLES. It "precompiles a smaller, simpler set of shaders at engine-build time so they don't compile at runtime" — which is why SkSL warm-up (`--cache-sksl`) is obsolete and first-run shader jank is largely gone. Disable with `--no-enable-impeller` or the `io.flutter.embedding.android.EnableImpeller` manifest meta-data.
(https://docs.flutter.dev/perf/impeller)

## 5. Measuring instead of guessing

**In the lab (DOCUMENTED).** `flutter run --profile` on a **physical device** — debug mode's asserts and JIT make its numbers meaningless. DevTools → Performance: the Flutter frames chart pairs a UI bar and a raster bar per frame; **frames over ~16 ms get a red overlay**, and frames doing shader compilation are marked **dark red**. "Enhance Tracing" adds *Track Widget Builds* (with widget names in the timeline), *Track Layouts* (shows intrinsic passes), and *Track Paints* — all three degrade frame times while enabled, so read them relatively. Rebuild Stats gives per-widget rebuild counts (the fastest way to find a `setState` scoped too high). Raster Stats breaks a slow frame into per-layer draw cost. Toggles for "Render Clip layers", "Render Opacity layers", "Render Physical Shape layers" isolate which effect is responsible. Timeline Events shows everything including custom `dart:developer` `Timeline`/`TimelineTask` spans — wrap each sync phase (drain outbox, catch-up fetch, apply) in one so sync work shows up on the same timeline as the frames it janks.
(https://docs.flutter.dev/tools/devtools/performance)

**In the field (DOCUMENTED).** `SchedulerBinding.instance.addTimingsCallback` delivers `FrameTiming` objects with `buildDuration` (UI thread), `rasterDuration` (raster thread), `totalSpan` (vsync start → raster finish) and `vsyncOverhead` (vsync signal → build start). The API docs are explicit that debug-mode numbers "may be very different" from profile/release. `addTimingsCallback` is preferred over `PlatformDispatcher.onReportTimings` because it supports multiple listeners. This is the only way to know what a mid-range Android phone on a train actually experiences: aggregate p50/p95/p99 of `totalSpan` and a jank-frame ratio per screen, batch them, and ship them with the same outbox that ships everything else.
(https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/dart-ui/FrameTiming-class.html)

sources.what: connectivity_plus README (why connectivity state is not a gate)
sources.key_fact: 'Connection type availability does not guarantee that there is an Internet access... You should not rely on the current connectivity status to decide whether you can reliably make a network request. Always guard your app code against timeouts and errors.' Android equivalent: NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET (claims internet) must be paired with NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED (OS actually probed), and even both together do not guarantee a usable path.

invariants: Every write has a client-generated stable id (UUID) created before any network attempt. That id is simultaneously the primary key, the retry idempotency key, and the dedupe key against the server echo — so at-least-once delivery becomes exactly-once observed state, and a retry after an ambiguous timeout is safe by construction.

The entity row and its outbox row are written in ONE local transaction. There is no window in which the user sees a message that nothing is responsible for sending, and no window in which something is queued that the UI does not show.

The server is the sole authority on order. Every replicated row carries a server-assigned monotonic position (Signal: server-ordered delivery; Telegram: pts/qts/seq; Linear: lastSyncId; PowerSync: bucket op id). Clients never invent ordering from local clocks, so two clients that have applied the same cursor range have byte-identical history.

Gaps are detected arithmetically, not probabilistically. Because positions are dense and monotonic, `expected == received` is a decidable local check: equal → apply, lower → already applied, discard idempotently, higher → a hole exists, fetch the difference. There is no 'probably fine' branch.

The persisted cursor advances only AFTER the local apply has committed. Crash between fetch and apply replays; it never skips. (PowerSync makes this explicit with checkpoint boundaries: data is only made visible at a consistent checkpoint, never mid-stream.)

Per-logical-stream serialisation, global parallelism. Signal's queue key is the recipient, so ordering is guaranteed exactly where it is observable and nowhere else. One stuck conversation cannot stall another.

Retry policy is declarative and bounded on two axes independently: attempts (Signal: UNLIMITED) and wall-clock lifespan (Signal: 24 h). A job that can never succeed still terminates, and termination is a state, not a silence.

A failed operation is a persisted row state (`sent_failed`), not a caught exception, not a toast, not an in-memory flag. It survives process death, it is visible in the same list the user was already looking at, and it carries a retry affordance. Signal's onFailure() writing markAsSentFailed to the DB is the canonical form.

Optimistic local state outranks stale server state for values the client has not yet had acknowledged (Figma: 'discard incoming changes from the server that conflict with unacknowledged property changes'). Otherwise the UI flickers back to the old value between send and ack.

Every catch-up path has a defined bailout to full resync when the incremental path is too far behind (Telegram: differenceTooLong / ChannelDifferenceTooLong; PowerSync: checksum mismatch → drop bucket and re-sync; Figma: download a fresh document). Unbounded history replay is never the fallback.

Retry timing is randomised so that N clients recovering from the same outage do not re-converge (AWS Full Jitter; Signal's ±25% proportional jitter). Correlated retry after a shared outage is the load spike, not the outage itself.
Connectivity state is an optimisation input (wake the drainer early), never a correctness gate. The authority on 'can I reach the server' is a request that succeeded or timed out.

Integrity of compacted state is verifiable without having witnessed the compaction (WhatsApp's homomorphic LtHash16 over snapshots; PowerSync's per-bucket checksums). A client that was offline for a month can accept a server-built snapshot and still prove nothing was silently dropped.
failure_modes_they_designed_for: Process death mid-send. Linear serialises transactions to IndexedDB before dispatch; Signal persists jobs to SQLite and restores them via BootReceiver + JobMigrator across app upgrades. An in-memory queue loses the user's message with no trace — the single most common local-first bug.

Ambiguous timeout: the request landed but the response did not. Solved by the client-generated id + idempotent server insert. Linear's write-up flags exactly this hole ('the client sends a transaction... but the window closes before receiving a response') as a source of non-idempotent resubmission errors.
Server echo arriving before, after, or instead of the ack. Same-id dedupe means the optimistic row is reconciled rather than duplicated, whichever arrives first.

The message emitted into a socket that no longer exists. Realtime pub/sub has no replay: a change published between socket-drop (T0) and resubscribe (T2) is delivered to nobody and never re-emitted. Every one of these systems answers with a durable ordered log plus a persisted cursor, queried on reconnect — never with 'resubscribe and hope'.
Redelivery after reconnect. Telegram's local_seq+1 > seq_start branch drops already-applied updates; without it, catch-up duplicates every message that arrived in the overlap window.
Offline longer than the retention of the incremental log. Handled by an explicit too-long signal and full/partial re-bootstrap rather than an unbounded backfill.
Correlated retry storms after a shared outage (the train-carriage-exiting-a-tunnel case). Full Jitter; backoff reset on request success rather than on a connectivity event.
Head-of-line blocking. Per-recipient/per-conversation queue keys mean one undeliverable message blocks exactly one conversation.

Battery and radio cost of futile attempts. NetworkConstraint gating means jobs are not even attempted without a network; Doze-aware push priority means the radio wakes only for things that produce user-visible output — FCM actively deprioritises senders that abuse this, using 7 days of history.

Silent socket death with no error. Supabase documents this explicitly for backgrounded apps: throttled heartbeat timers → server assumes disconnect → 'your application then stops receiving events without any explicit error message'. Designed-for answer is an application-level liveness check (heartbeat callback / cursor probe on resume), not trusting the socket's own state.

Credential expiry across an offline window. A 1-hour JWT expiring while the device is in a tunnel means the socket reconnects with a dead token; the refreshed token must be pushed into the realtime layer explicitly.

Concurrent edits to the same value. Deliberately NOT solved by merge in Figma's case — atomic per-property LWW means 'the result is always one client's complete value, never a merge', and they accept that simultaneous text editing of one value does not work rather than pay for OT/CRDT.
A malformed or unparseable row poisoning the whole catch-up batch. Robust clients skip the row and continue rather than aborting the sync.
research.applicability_to_supabase:
"## What I found in the actual codebase (E:\LDR\mobile)

**There is no local database.** `pubspec.yaml` lists no drift / isar / hive / objectbox / sembast; `sqflite` appears only transitively in `pubspec.lock`. Persistence is `shared_preferences` and `flutter_secure_storage`. `ChatRepository.fetch()` does `.select().limit(500)` straight from PostgREST on screen open, and `ChatSendQueue._pending` is a plain `List<PendingSend>` in a singleton — **gone on process death, with the user's photo in it**. This is the read-the-network-in-the-UI architecture that every system above moved away from.

**One concrete correctness bug, worth fixing before anything else.** `lib/features/chat/chat_screen.dart` lines ~125-129:

```dart
try {
  await ChatRepository.sendText(coupleId, body, id: id, replyToId: replyId);
} catch (_) {
  /* it's already on screen; the DB retry isn't worth blocking */
}
```

The optimistic bubble is already rendered AND the text has already been fanned out to the partner over `sendBroadcastMessage`. So when the insert fails, the partner has *seen* the message, the sender *sees* the message, and it exists in no database. On next launch both sides lose it — with no error at any point. This is the exact failure mode Signal designed `onFailure() → markAsSentFailed(messageId)` to make impossible. Two fixes, in order: (1) the catch must set a `failed` status on the local row and surface a retry, exactly like `ChatSendQueue` already does for media; (2) the broadcast should not fire until the insert commits, or the partner should treat broadcast-only messages as provisional until the postgres echo confirms them.

**What is already right and should be built on, not replaced.** `ChatRepository.fetchSince(coupleId, afterSeq)` — `.gt('seq', afterSeq).order('seq').limit(500)` — is a proper monotonic sync cursor, and the comment above it correctly diagnoses the socket-drop/resubscribe gap that Telegram's `getDifference` exists to solve. The client-generated `Uuid().v4()` shared across the optimistic row, the broadcast payload, and the DB insert is exactly the idempotency key the pattern needs. The `seq` column is the local equivalent of `pts`/`lastSyncId`. **The primitives exist; they are just not persisted and not universal.**

## What transfers directly, free tier, no new service

1. **Make `seq` durable.** Persist `last_seq` per couple to disk (SQLite, or `shared_preferences` as a stopgap), not to a screen's state. On resume/reconnect/FCM-tickle: `fetchSince(persisted_seq)`, apply, then advance the cursor — apply-then-advance, never the reverse. This alone converts your realtime channel from a source of truth into a latency optimisation, which is what it should be.
2. **Idempotent server insert.** Change the inserts in `chat_repository.dart` (lines 228, 249, 279, 309) to `upsert(..., ignoreDuplicates: true)` on the `id` PK, or an RPC doing `insert ... on conflict (id) do nothing`. Without this, retrying an ambiguous timeout is a 23505 and your outbox can never be safely aggressive.
3. **A real outbox table** in local SQLite (drift is the sane choice for a Flutter+Riverpod codebase; you already have sqflite transitively). Schema mirroring Signal's Job.Parameters: `id, couple_id, kind, payload, queue_key, attempt, next_attempt_at, expires_at, status`. Write the message row and the outbox row in one `db.transaction`. A single drainer isolate/timer pulls due rows ordered by `next_attempt_at`, serialised per `queue_key`. Signal's exact policy is a good starting point: `lifespan = 24h`, unlimited attempts within it, `backoff = min(2^attempt * 1000, 30_000) * (0.75 + rand()*0.5)` — or upgrade to AWS Full Jitter, `random(0, min(30_000, 1000 * 2^attempt))`, which is strictly better under correlated recovery and is the same three lines.
4. **Unify media and text through it.** Right now `ChatSendQueue` handles image/video with retry, and text and voice bypass it entirely (`sendVoice` goes straight through the repository, and the comment in `chat_send_queue.dart` says so). One outbox, all kinds, one status column driving one UI treatment.
5. **`sendStatus` is already rendered** (`chat_screen.dart` ~line 1644 branches on `SendStatus.failed`). Once the status lives in SQLite instead of a singleton list, that UI keeps working and starts surviving restarts for free.
6. **Connectivity as a wake signal only.** `connectivity_plus` events reset the drainer's timer; they must not gate the request, per the package's own README. Reset backoff on a *successful* request, not on a connectivity event — otherwise every device leaving the same tunnel resets to zero attempt simultaneously.
7. **Request coalescing.** Keep a `Map<String, Future<T>>` of in-flight catch-ups keyed by `coupleId`. `onResume` + connectivity change + `subscribe` callback all fire within ~200 ms of leaving a tunnel and would otherwise produce three identical `.gt('seq', ...)` queries. Same for session refresh.
8. **`supabase.realtime.setAuth(freshToken)` after every token refresh, and unconditionally on resume.** The default JWT is 3600 s and the client refreshes ~60 s before expiry — a device offline across that boundary reconnects with a dead token and the channel errors. This is a documented, still-open sharp edge (supabase/realtime-js#274, supabase-flutter#1012).
9. **Treat FCM as a tickle, not a transport.** Max 4 collapse keys, max 100 stored messages per disconnected instance, TTL up to 28 days. Send a data message with a collapse key per couple carrying nothing but 'there is news' — the client answers by running `fetchSince(persisted_seq)`. That makes the 100-message cap irrelevant and means you never have to make push payloads reliable.

## What CRDTs are and are not worth here

Don't. Chat is an append-only per-author log with a server-assigned `seq` — the hard part of CRDTs (concurrent convergent edits to a shared mutable structure) does not arise. Figma, running a far more concurrent product, explicitly chose server-authoritative per-property LWW over both OT and CRDTs and gave the reason: with an authoritative server the extra machinery buys nothing. Your mutable-shared-state surfaces (couple settings, chat theme, shared lists in `together`/`rituals`) are per-property LWW cases: add `updated_at` per field or per row and let last write win. The only place a CRDT would earn its keep is a genuinely co-edited long-lived document, and Dart's Automerge/Yjs bindings are not mature enough to take that bet on.

## What needs a paid tier

- **Realtime concurrent connections.** Free = 200. Both partners connected means ~100 couples online simultaneously. 'Thousands of users' is a hard wall you hit long before any other limit. Pro = 500, Pro-without-spend-cap/Team = 10,000.
- **Broadcast payload.** 256 KB on Free vs 3,000 KB on Pro. Your `_moodChannel` text broadcast is fine; anything richer is not.
- **Messages/sec.** Free = 100/s project-wide, joins 100/s. A reconnect stampede (everyone's commute ending) is measured in channel joins, and 100/s is not much when 200 sockets all reconnect at once — jitter your own channel subscribe, not just your HTTP retries.

## What does not exist yet and must be built or bought

- **A local database and a sync engine.** This is the whole gap. Either build the minimum (drift + outbox + persisted cursor + drainer, roughly the shape above — this is maybe 600 lines and it is the highest-leverage work available on this codebase), or adopt **PowerSync**, which has a first-class Flutter SDK and a documented Supabase integration and gives you buckets/checkpoints/upload-queue/write-checkpoint semantics off the shelf. PowerSync is a service and costs money past its free tier; the DIY version costs engineering time but keeps you on the free tier.
- **A durable per-recipient server queue.** Supabase Realtime does not have one and never will — it is fire-and-forget pub/sub with no replay. Your `messages` table plus `seq` IS the durable ordered log. That is the correct substitute; the job is to actually treat it as such rather than as a backup for the socket.
- **Server-side fanout that doesn't melt.** Move off `postgres_changes` to **Broadcast from Database** (`realtime.broadcast_changes()` in an AFTER trigger on `messages`, private channel `couple:{id}`, RLS policy on `realtime.messages`). See scale notes — this is not an optimisation, it is the difference between working and not working at your target size.
- **Field telemetry.** Nothing in the app records `FrameTiming`. Add a `SchedulerBinding.instance.addTimingsCallback` that buckets `totalSpan` per route and ships p50/p95/p99 + jank-frame ratio through the same outbox. You have three real test devices (IN2015 / Vivo / OnePlus 7) but you will never reproduce a train on your desk.

## Flutter specifics against this codebase

- `chat_screen.dart` is **2,118 lines**. The rebuild-scoping problem is structural: a `setState` anywhere in that State rebuilds everything. Split the message list, the input bar, and the header into separate widgets subscribing to narrow Riverpod providers; use `Rebuild Stats` in DevTools to confirm rather than assume.
- The chat list should be `ListView.builder(reverse: true)` with `addRepaintBoundaries: true` (default). Default `cacheExtent` is **250.0 logical pixels** — for chat bubbles that is only ~2-3 extra bubbles per edge, which is right; do not raise it globally to 'smooth' scrolling, that just moves the cost.
- Bubbles must not trigger `saveLayer`. Rounded corners via `borderRadius` on the decoration, not `ClipRRect` with `Clip.antiAliasWithSaveLayer`. Semi-transparent overlays via a colour with alpha, not `Opacity`.
- Images: your recent commit 'stop paying 4K for a photo shown in a 220dp bubble' is the right fix — confirm every `Image.network`/`Image.file` in `media_viewer.dart` and the bubble path passes `cacheWidth`/`cacheHeight` at device-pixel size. Default `ImageCache` is **1000 images / 100 MB**, which on a 3 GB phone in a photo-heavy chat is a plausible OOM; consider lowering `maximumSizeBytes` and note that `clear()` does not evict live images.
- Isolates: the `cryptography` package work for the Closer/Vault E2EE module and any image encode/resize belong off the main isolate. `Isolate.run` per call is fine for a one-off unlock; use a **long-lived** isolate for per-message encrypt/decrypt, because spawn + argument copy per message will cost more than the crypto. Remember a background isolate cannot host a platform-channel listener.
- `google_mobile_ads` is in the dependency list. Ad SDK work on the platform thread is a classic raster/UI stall — measure `FrameTiming` with ads on and off before blaming your own code."
research.scale_notes:
"**The binding constraint for this app is Supabase Postgres Changes, and it is much tighter than the connection cap.** Documented: 'Postgres Changes authorizes every event against each subscriber' — one change with 100 subscribers = 100 RLS evaluations — and changes are 'processed on a single thread to preserve their order, which means larger compute add-ons don't meaningfully increase Postgres Changes throughput.' Published Micro-instance benchmarks WITH RLS: 500 clients → 30 DB changes/sec; 1,500 clients → 10/sec; 3,000 clients → **5 DB changes/sec for the entire project**. For a couple app the fanout per message is only 2, so fanout is not what kills you — the single-threaded, RLS-per-subscriber WAL processor shared across every couple is. At 1,000 concurrent devices you are looking at roughly 10-30 changes/sec *total*, i.e. under one message per second per hundred active users. Supabase's own guidance: above ~3,000 concurrent subscribers on the same changes, use Broadcast. **Migrate to `realtime.broadcast_changes()` from an AFTER trigger, on private channels, before you scale — not after.** Broadcast authorises at channel join and caches the policy for the connection lifetime instead of re-checking per event, and `realtime.messages` is daily-partitioned with 3-day auto-drop so it does not grow unbounded.

**Free-tier Realtime ceiling: 200 concurrent connections.** With both partners online that is ~100 simultaneously active couples, and it is a hard cap, not a soft degradation. Pro is 500; Pro-without-spend-cap and Team are 10,000. 'Thousands of users' means Pro-without-spend-cap at minimum. Secondary free-tier limits: 100 messages/sec and 100 channel joins/sec project-wide — the joins limit is what a synchronised reconnect (commute ending, or a Supabase restart) actually saturates, so client-side jitter on `subscribe()` matters as much as jitter on HTTP retries.

**Where the DIY sync engine breaks.** A drift-backed outbox + `seq` cursor scales essentially forever on the client side; the cost is engineering time and the specific bugs the pattern exists to prevent (cursor advanced before apply, non-idempotent retry, unbounded backfill). Two concrete limits to design around now: (a) `fetchSince` uses `.limit(500)` — a client offline for a week needs *paged* catch-up looping until a short page, plus a 'too far behind' bailout that drops local history and re-bootstraps, which is Telegram's `differenceTooLong` and PowerSync's checksum-mismatch path; (b) deletes need tombstones or the cursor cannot express them — PowerSync's rule is a row is removed only when removed from all buckets, and your equivalent is a `deleted_at` column that `fetchSince` returns rather than a hard DELETE, or you get rows that resurrect on reinstall. Your existing `deleteForEveryone` RPC needs checking against this.

**Where PowerSync sits.** Documented to scale to 'tens of thousands of concurrent clients per PowerSync Service instance' and hundreds of thousands to a million+ rows per client, and it gives you checkpoints, checksums, upload queue and LSN-backed write confirmation for free. Cost: another paid service, another deployment, and its sync-rule model has to be expressed for every table you want offline. For a two-person-per-tenant app with a handful of tables, the DIY version is genuinely simpler and stays on the free tier — the case for PowerSync gets strong only if you want *every* feature (vault, timeline, rituals, capsule) offline-first rather than just chat.

**Where CRDTs break.** Metadata overhead grows with edit history, not document size; Dart bindings are immature; and for LWW-shaped data they buy nothing over a server-assigned order. Figma runs a far more concurrent product on per-property LWW. Cost of adopting one here would be high and the benefit is zero for chat.

**Flutter-side ceilings.** The 16 ms budget is per-frame and non-negotiable; the practical split is ~8 ms UI + ~8 ms raster, halving to 8 ms total on 120 Hz hardware. Impeller (default from 3.27 on API 29+) removed shader-compilation jank as a class of problem, so the remaining jank sources are yours: oversized `build()` scopes, intrinsic layout passes (two passes, polling all cells), `saveLayer`, and full-resolution image decode. `ImageCache`'s 100 MB / 1000-image default is generous enough to be an OOM risk on the low-end devices in your test set. Isolate spawn + message copy is not free — per-message crypto or per-thumbnail resize through `Isolate.run` will cost more in copying than it saves, so long-lived isolates for anything repeated.

**Backoff economics.** AWS's own simulation is honest that jitter does not change the O(N²) nature of contention — it halves the calls and stops the synchronised spike. At your scale the spike is what matters (200 sockets reconnecting inside the same second), not steady-state throughput. Full Jitter, `random(0, min(cap, base*2^attempt))`, with cap around 30 s, is the right default; Signal's ±25% proportional jitter is weaker but already 10× better than none.

**Cost of doing nothing.** Today: any message whose insert fails is silently lost after having been shown to both users; any send in flight when the process dies is lost with no trace; and every screen open costs a 500-row network round-trip before anything renders. None of those get better with more users — the last one gets linearly worse in egress and in cold-start latency, and the first two get more frequent as your user base moves onto worse networks than yours."

modules.name: Sign-up + email confirmation
modules.purpose: Create an auth account with email/password and get the user back into the app after they tap the confirmation link.

modules.tables: auth.users (GoTrue). Trigger public.handle_new_user (E:/LDR/supabase/schema.sql l.267-288) inserts public.profiles(id, display_name=email local-part, timezone='UTC'). trg_init_presence (E:/LDR/supabase/20260628_presence_repair_trigger.sql l.50-70) then inserts public.presence(user_id, couple_id=null).
modules.realtime_or_push: None. Pure HTTPS to GoTrue. Confirmation return path is an Android deep link (custom scheme 'tethered'), parsed in-process by supabase_flutter, which then emits an onAuthStateChange event consumed by SessionNotifier.
modules.current_mechanism: signUp() calls _c.auth.signUp(email, password, emailRedirectTo: 'tethered://auth-callback'). The page does NOT navigate on success — it just sets a text notice 'Check your inbox'. Whether a session exists immediately depends entirely on the Supabase project's 'Confirm email' dashboard setting, which is not in this repo. Two DB triggers fire on the auth.users insert: handle_new_user creates a bare profile (display_name defaults to the part of the email before '@'), init_presence_on_profile creates a presence row. Tapping the mail link opens MainActivity via the tethered://auth-callback intent-filter; supabase_flutter strips the tokens off the URL itself (main.dart:378-384 explicitly ignores this host) and fires AuthChangeEvent.signedIn, which SessionNotifier.init's listener turns into loadProfile(), which makes the router funnel run.
modules.known_weaknesses: (1) Cold-start trap: if the app is not already running, the confirmation link launches the process and MilesApp.showRealApp starts false (main.dart:97), so the user lands on the fake News cover with a valid session and no visible way in. Nothing on the cover hints at the 5-logo-tap / search-'home' / 2.5s-long-press triggers, and a brand-new user has never been told them. (2) No resend-confirmation path anywhere in the client. (3) No client-side password strength/format validation on sign-up beyond the hint text — errors come back from the server and are string-matched in features/auth/auth_errors.dart. (4) The default display_name leaks the email local-part into a profile the partner can read. (5) friendlyAuthError does substring matching on lowercased exception text — brittle across GoTrue versions.
modules.scale_reason: The mechanism itself is stateless HTTPS and scales, but the cold-start-behind-the-disguise dead end converts a normal confirmation flow into a support ticket for a meaningful fraction of new users, and there is no resend path to recover.

modules.tables: auth.users; then public.profiles + public.couples read by SessionNotifier.loadProfile.
modules.realtime_or_push: None for the sign-in itself. Immediately after, loadProfile subscribes a Postgres-changes channel 'profile-sync:<coupleId>' (supabase_repository.dart l.449-474) and writes presence.

(2) On failure the page only shows a mapped string; there is no lockout/backoff client-side and no evidence of one server-side beyond GoTrue defaults. The navigation happens invisibly; after passing the cover trigger the user may or may not still be on /new-password because passwordRecovery is consumed (set false) on the first notification. (2) The recovery-session route guard is path-based only: any later navigation away from /new-password loses the exemption and the funnel takes over. (4) No re-authentication requirement to change a password from an already-signed-in session; there is no change-password UI in settings at all.

modules.name: Session bootstrap and state machine (SessionNotifier)

modules.tables: public.profiles (self, via .eq('id',uid)), public.couples (via .eq('id', profile.couple_id)), public.profiles again for the partner (.eq('couple_id').neq('id',uid)), public.presence (integrity read + repair write + setOnline).

Requires a live websocket; a missed reconnect means a frozen partner avatar/name/status until reconnectPresence() runs from realtime resume.

EVERY auth event with a non-null session (including tokenRefreshed, roughly hourly) calls loadProfile(). loadProfile does up to 5 sequential round trips with 10s timeouts each: profiles select, couples select, partner profiles select, presence couple_id verify, presence repair/setOnline. The listener at session_provider.dart l.71-74 therefore keeps the dead session, isAuthenticated stays true, the router never sends the user to /signin, and every PostgREST call 401s forever until the app is killed and relaunched. (4) The presence 'integrity guard' (l.172-195) is an unconditional extra read+write on every load, per user, forever — the comment openly calls it '~200ms on every app load'. modules.name: Profile creation and timezone
modules.purpose: Capture display name, timezone and date of birth (18+ gate), which is what marks onboarding complete.
modules.entry_points: E:/LDR/mobile/lib/features/auth/welcome_page.dart (_submit l.74-115); supabase_repository.dart upsertProfile (l.100-115) and updateMyProfile (l.307-320); session_provider.dart syncTimezone (l.98-110); settings_screen.dart _changeTimezone (l.236-252); E:/LDR/mobile/lib/core/time/tz_helper.dart deviceZone (l.60-77); commonTimezones list in core/config.dart (17 entries)
modules.tables: public.profiles — columns id, display_name, timezone, presence_status, birth_date (added by E:/LDR/supabase/intimacy_additions.sql l.10-11), status_message (settings_and_delete.sql l.4). CHECK constraint profiles_must_be_adult (intimacy_additions.sql l.20-32).
modules.realtime_or_push: Writes propagate to the partner over the 'profile-sync:<coupleId>' Postgres-changes channel. No push.
modules.current_mechanism: upsertProfile does a PostgREST upsert on profiles with id=auth.uid(), display_name, timezone, presence_status='free', birth_date. RLS profiles_insert_self/profiles_update_self allow it; column-level UPDATE grants are rebuilt from information_schema by hardening_couple_id_fix.sql l.28-43 and again by newuser_fixes.sql l.162-173, excluding couple_id. Timezone is guessed by matching the device's current UTC offset against the 17-entry commonTimezones list — offset matching, so any zone sharing an offset is a coin flip. syncTimezone re-runs on every app resume and silently rewrites profiles.timezone when the device offset maps to a different list entry.
modules.known_weaknesses: (1) The DOB is the onboarding flag; there is no explicit onboarded column. (2) The timezone list is 17 cities worldwide — a user in, say, Africa/Lagos or America/Bogota is assigned whichever listed zone happens to share their offset today, and syncTimezone will flip it twice a year at DST boundaries because it matches on current offset, not zone identity. (3) syncTimezone fires unconditionally on resume and, when it disagrees, does an UPDATE plus a full loadProfile (another 5 round trips). (4) Age is computed from the device clock in welcome_page._age (l.44-53) — a rolled-back device clock passes the client gate; only the DB CHECK constraint stops the write, and its failure surfaces as the generic 'Something went wrong'. (5) No way to change display_name/DOB pre-pairing except via Settings, which is unreachable while the funnel holds you.
modules.scale_reason: Correctness degrades for most of the world's timezones, and the resume-triggered sync amplifies the loadProfile fan-out. Writes themselves are cheap.

modules.name: Couple creation and pairing invites
modules.purpose: Link exactly two profiles into one couple via an expiring single-use code or deep link.
modules.entry_points: E:/LDR/mobile/lib/features/auth/couple_page.dart (_restoreInvite l.52-64, _create l.72-90, _join l.92-111, _enterApp l.130-133, inviteLinkFor l.19); supabase_repository.dart activePairingInvite (l.243-257), createPairingInvite (l.261-273), redeemPairingInvite (l.277-302), createCouple (l.190-200, now dead — no callers); main.dart _handleLink (l.378-384); E:/LDR/mobile/lib/features/home/home_screen.dart _WaitingForPartnerState (l.409-445)
modules.tables: public.pairing_invites (code PK, couple_id, created_by, created_at, expires_at, consumed_at, consumed_by) — E:/LDR/supabase/pairing_invites.sql; public.couples; public.profiles.couple_id. RPCs: create_pairing_invite (current definition E:/LDR/supabase/newuser_fixes.sql l.50-87, superseding pairing_invites.sql l.25-56), redeem_pairing_invite (pairing_invites.sql l.60-89). join_couple_by_code was DROPPED by hardening_2026_08.sql l.85 and couples.invite_code was nulled and made nullable (l.91-92).
modules.realtime_or_push: None. The inviter learns their partner joined only by polling — i.e. by loadProfile running on resume or token refresh. There is no realtime subscription on pairing_invites or on couples, and no push.
modules.current_mechanism: 'Create & get a code' calls create_pairing_invite (SECURITY DEFINER): if the caller has no couple it INSERTS one and links their profile, then mints an 8-char code from a 31-symbol ambiguity-free alphabet with a 24h TTL. The invite is re-read from the server on screen re-entry via activePairingInvite (RLS pairing_invites_select_member scopes it to the caller's couple). 'Join' calls redeem_pairing_invite, which validates existence, consumed_at, expires_at, self-couple, already_paired and a >=2 member cap, then updates profiles.couple_id as the definer (bypassing trg_guard_couple_id, which only refuses writes where current_user is 'authenticated'/'anon'). tethered://join?code=XXXX is caught by app_links, uppercased into pendingInviteCodeProvider and the router is pushed to /couple.
modules.known_weaknesses: (1) STRUCTURAL TRAP: tapping 'Create' silently creates a real couple and links you to it. From then on redeem_pairing_invite raises 'already_paired', and the CouplePage swaps the join field out for the invite-reveal view — so if BOTH partners tap Create, neither can join the other and the only recovery is Settings → Disconnect (leave_couple). _restoreInvite reproduces the reveal on every relaunch, so restarting does not help. (2) activePairingInvite filters `expires_at > DateTime.now().toUtc()` computed on the DEVICE (supabase_repository.dart l.248) — a skewed phone clock hides its own live invite or shows an expired one. (3) The inviter has no live signal that the partner joined; they sit on _WaitingForPartner until something else triggers loadProfile. (4) No rate limit on redeem_pairing_invite; distinct error strings (invalid_code / expired / already_used / couple_full) are a clean oracle, mitigated only by the 40-bit code space. (5) createCouple + the create_couple RPC are still deployed but have zero callers. (6) The 2-member cap is a `select count(*)` with no unique constraint or lock — two simultaneous redemptions of two different invites for the same couple can both pass the check.
modules.scale_reason: Both-create deadlock and the clock-dependent expiry check are user-visible failures that need manual recovery; the unlocked member-count check is a genuine race that only appears under concurrency; and the inviter's 'did they join yet' answer is delivered by polling a 5-query loadProfile.

modules.name: Leaving a couple
modules.purpose: Dissolve the pairing and wipe the shared presence surface.
modules.tables: Current definition E:/LDR/supabase/20260628_leave_couple_privacy.sql (supersedes settings_and_delete.sql l.8-17 and 20260627_leave_couple_fix.sql). Touches public.presence (17 columns nulled), public.profiles.couple_id for BOTH members, public.couples.active=false. Client then also PATCHes public.presence itself and calls auth.refreshSession().
modules.realtime_or_push: No notification to the other partner at all. They discover it when their own loadProfile next runs and returns couple_id=null — which then funnels them to /couple with no explanation.
modules.current_mechanism: SECURITY DEFINER leave_couple(): clears the sensitive presence columns FIRST (ordering matters — trg_sync_presence_couple_id nulls presence.couple_id the instant profiles.couple_id changes, which would make the WHERE match zero rows), then nulls couple_id on both profiles, then flags couples.active=false. Client follows with a best-effort presence PATCH and a refreshSession() so the token-refresh event re-runs loadProfile into a clean no-couple state. Messages, capsules, vault rows and storage objects are all deliberately preserved.
modules.known_weaknesses: (1) Unilateral and silent — either partner can dissolve the couple and the other gets no message, just a funnel bounce. (2) couples.active is written but read by nothing in the Flutter client (grep: no reader), so dissolved couples and all their rows accumulate forever. (3) All chat/media/vault rows for the dead couple survive with no owner and no retention policy. (4) leaveCouple relies on a refreshSession() side effect to re-drive the session; if that call fails offline the client is left with a stale couple in memory until the next resume. (5) Nothing invalidates the dead couple's outstanding pairing_invites rows.
modules.scale_reason: Unbounded orphaned data (couples, messages, storage objects) with no reaper, plus a silent state change for the other party that the router turns into an unexplained onboarding bounce.

modules.name: Account deletion
modules.purpose: Play-policy-required in-app permanent deletion of the account and its data.
modules.entry_points: settings_screen.dart _deleteAccount (l.343-404, requires typing DELETE); supabase_repository.dart deleteMyAccount (l.207-208)
modules.tables: RPC public.delete_my_account (E:/LDR/supabase/account_deletion.sql). Reads profiles.couple_id, counts remaining members; if last member deletes storage.objects in buckets couple_media / couple_intimate / capsule-media plus rows in public.messages and public.couples; then `delete from auth.users where id = auth.uid()`, cascading to profiles and from there to every couple-scoped table. FK fixes so this can actually run are in newuser_fixes.sql l.17-38 (pairing_invites.consumed_by/created_by were NO ACTION and blocked deletion).
modules.realtime_or_push: None. The partner is not notified.
modules.current_mechanism: Client clears the FCM token, calls the RPC, then SessionNotifier.signOut() and go('/signin'). Storage cleanup is wrapped in `exception when others then null` so a storage failure cannot strand the user.
modules.known_weaknesses: (1) Synchronous single-transaction delete that touches storage.objects with a join against messages — this is a long transaction, unbatched, on the request path. (2) Everything runs as one all-or-nothing statement: any FK added later with NO ACTION against profiles silently reintroduces the guaranteed-failure bug that newuser_fixes.sql l.10-38 documents (the joiner in EVERY couple could not delete their account). (3) The user's JWT stays cryptographically valid until expiry (~1h) after the row is gone — PostgREST only verifies the signature. (4) If the partner is still in the couple, the deleting user's messages remain (only the last member's deletion removes them) despite the dialog copy saying 'permanently deletes … your messages'. (5) Local device state (app-lock PIN + enabled flag, disguise choice, setup_completed_once, perms_requested_v1) is untouched by deletion.
modules.scale_reason: Correct in the common path but it is an unbatched multi-table + storage delete inside one request-scoped transaction; at volume this is a lock and timeout source, and the FK fragility is a repeat offender.

modules.name: App lock (biometric + PIN)
modules.purpose: A second gate over the real app after the disguise cover, and on resume.
modules.entry_points: E:/LDR/mobile/lib/core/services/app_lock.dart; E:/LDR/mobile/lib/core/widgets/lock_screen.dart; E:/LDR/mobile/lib/core/widgets/app_lock_pin_sheet.dart; toggled in settings_screen.dart _toggleAppLock (l.85-110); raised from main.dart initState l.152-153 and didChangeAppLifecycleState l.278-283; consulted by the cover gate (cover_gate.dart l.72-73, fake_news_screen.dart l.153-155)
modules.tables: NONE. Entirely SharedPreferences: 'app_lock_enabled' (bool) and 'app_lock_pin_hash' (sha256 of 'miles-applock::'+pin). Nothing server-side.
modules.realtime_or_push: None.
modules.current_mechanism: local_auth authenticate() with biometricOnly:false (so the device credential is an accepted fallback) and stickyAuth:true; MainActivity extends FlutterFragmentActivity, which is what makes the prompt possible at all. A 4-digit PIN is mandatory when enabling the lock so there is always a non-biometric way in. AppLock.locked is a ValueNotifier rendered as a top-of-stack overlay in main.dart l.492-498; LockScreen wraps itself in PopScope(canPop:false).
modules.known_weaknesses: (1) Device-local only, so it survives nothing: android:allowBackup="false" plus fullBackupContent="false" (AndroidManifest l.85-87) means a reinstall wipes both the enabled flag and the PIN hash — the app lock is simply gone, and the account is protected by the password alone. (2) A 4-digit PIN hashed with a single unsalted SHA-256 pass is 10,000 candidates; anyone with the prefs file breaks it instantly. There is no attempt counter, no lockout, no delay. (3) The lock and the disguise cover are two independent gates with two independent enable states, and the biometric prompt is shared between them via the MilesApp.authInProgress static. (4) Nothing binds the lock to the signed-in identity — signing out and signing in as someone else keeps the same PIN.
modules.scale_reason: Purely client-side and per-device; no backend cost. The weaknesses are security and durability, not scale.

modules.current_mechanism: One <activity-alias> per identity; exactly one is enabled at a time via PackageManager.setComponentEnabledSetting (new one enabled BEFORE the others are disabled so the app can never vanish from the launcher). MainActivity itself carries no MAIN/LAUNCHER filter. DisguiseService.apply persists the choice first (the component switch can force-stop the process), and reconcile() on cold start queries the actually-enabled alias and repairs prefs drift, with a 2s timeout and a 3s outer timeout in DisguiseCoverHost. MilesApp.showRealApp starts false and is reset to false on paused/hidden/detached and (after a 300ms confirm) on inactive; only the cover gate sets it true, after AppLock and a 900ms-ish intro splash. MaterialApp title is deliberately '' in both branches so recents falls back to the alias label. Two extra layers ride on top: StealthLayer (invisible 48x48 top-right long-press → full-screen 'syncing' scrim, main.dart l.501) and EmergencyLockService (3 shakes in 1.5s, or volume up+down within 1s via the native miles/volume_keys channel → instant drop to cover).
modules.known_weaknesses: (1) The first-run exemption in didChangeAppLifecycleState (main.dart l.239-269) is a genuinely intricate piece of state — it depends on MilesApp.setupCompletedOnce (SharedPreferences), MilesApp.authInProgress and MilesApp.systemOverlayActive, three mutable statics that every picker/camera/permission call site must set and clear correctly by hand. A missed clear locks the user out or leaves the app uncovered. (2) FakeNewsScreen duplicates the CoverGate mixin rather than using it, so the two entry paths can drift. (3) The 'secret search word' is the literal string 'home' (fake_news_screen.dart l.202) — a plausible thing to type into a news search by accident. (4) Nothing tells a new user the trigger exists; combined with cold-start deep links this is the confirmation/recovery dead end. (5) The identity is device-local, so a reinstall reverts to News and the choice is lost. (6) The manifest label and disguise_profile.dart labels are kept in sync by hand.
modules.scale_reason: Zero backend involvement. The risk is UX lock-out and per-device state drift, not load.

modules.name: Device push-token binding (identity side)
modules.purpose: Associate this device's FCM token with the signed-in profile so pairing/reach/call/message pushes can reach it.
modules.entry_points: E:/LDR/mobile/lib/core/services/fcm_service.dart (registerToken l.84-100, _save l.102, clearToken l.111-116); supabase_repository.dart setFcmToken (l.392-400); called from app_shell _onReady after pairing, from main.dart on every resume (l.286), and cleared on sign-out (settings_screen.dart l.408, couple_page.dart l.122)
modules.tables: public.profiles.fcm_token + fcm_token_updated_at (fcm_token added by E:/LDR/supabase/fcm_push.sql l.7).
modules.realtime_or_push: This IS the push identity. Server-side notify triggers read profiles.fcm_token and call net.http_post (pg_net), and null the column when FCM answers UNREGISTERED.
modules.current_mechanism: getToken() with up to 4 attempts and 2s backoff, then a single UPDATE of profiles.fcm_token. Re-registered on every app resume specifically to self-heal a token the notify functions nulled.
modules.known_weaknesses: (1) ONE token column per profile — the schema physically cannot represent a user with two devices; the second device silently steals push from the first. (2) The token is stored on the same profiles row the partner can SELECT (profiles_select_self_or_partner grants the partner every column, including fcm_token) — the partner can read your device push token. (3) registerToken runs on every resume, so that is one profiles UPDATE per user per foreground event regardless of whether the token changed. (4) Sign-out clears the token only if the network call succeeds; a failed clearToken leaves the device receiving the previous account's pushes.
modules.scale_reason: Single-token-per-user is a schema-level ceiling that breaks multi-device outright, the partner-readable token is a privacy leak that RLS currently permits, and the per-resume write multiplies with user count.

modules.name: chat.transport (message delivery core)
modules.purpose: Get a message from one partner's phone onto the other's screen, and keep the on-screen list consistent with Postgres.
modules.entry_points: E:/LDR/mobile/lib/features/chat/chat_screen.dart (_subscribe L386-460, _onIncoming L512-549, _catchUp L368-384, _onMsgBroadcast L134-151, didChangeAppLifecycleState L321-333); E:/LDR/mobile/lib/features/chat/chat_repository.dart (subscribe L321-355, fetch L204-220, fetchSince L183-200); E:/LDR/mobile/lib/core/realtime_resume.dart; E:/LDR/mobile/lib/features/shell/app_shell.dart (_reconnectRealtime L69-79)
modules.tables: public.messages (id, couple_id, sender_id, body, image_path, voice_path, video_path, reply_to_id, kind, seq, created_at, deleted_for_everyone, deleted_by, deleted_at, sender_mood, sender_mood_color). Indexes: messages_couple_created_idx(couple_id, created_at), messages_couple_seq_idx(couple_id, seq). RLS via public.current_user_couple_id().
modules.realtime_or_push: THREE independent transports, all in use simultaneously. (1) Supabase Realtime BROADCAST on public topic 'mood_burst:<coupleId>' — carries text and image 'msg' events, typing, 'cleared', and mood/GIF bursts. Ephemeral, no persistence, no auth (see weaknesses). (2) postgres_changes on 'messages:<coupleId>' with filter couple_id=eq.<id>, INSERT + DELETE events. (3) FCM data push via a per-row AFTER INSERT trigger (see chat.push). Recovery is a plain REST catch-up query, not a transport.
modules.current_mechanism: On mount ChatScreen fetches the newest 300 rows ordered by created_at desc (ChatRepository.fetch, hard limit 300, NO pagination — older history is unreachable in the UI). It then calls _subscribe(), which awaits removeChannel() on the three previous channels before joining fresh ones (Supabase never dedupes by topic, so unsubscribe+rejoin left dead channels). Both broadcast and postgres_changes fire _onIncoming; dedupe is by message id held in an in-memory Set<String> _ids. A broadcast-delivered message is constructed client-side with seq=0; when the slower Postgres echo arrives with the same id, Message.reconcileWith() adopts the server's created_at, paths, deletion flags and seq. Because both realtime paths are live-only (their cursor is the moment of join), _catchUp() issues a REST SELECT ... where seq > _maxSeq order by seq limit 500 on every socket re-open (realtimeResumed fires from realtime.onOpen) and on every app resume. _maxSeq is a fold over the whole in-memory list on every access. Every _onIncoming does setState + a full _sortMessages() re-sort of the entire list.
modules.known_weaknesses: The broadcast topic 'mood_burst:<coupleId>' is a PUBLIC Realtime channel — no `private: true` anywhere in lib/, and no realtime.messages RLS in any SQL file. couple_id is not secret (it is the first path segment of every never-expiring public couple_media URL, as hardening_2026_08.sql L25 itself admits). Any client that knows a couple_id can join the topic and (a) read every text message and image path in real time, (b) inject a forged 'msg' with an arbitrary 'sender' — _onMsgBroadcast L134-151 does no membership or sender check, and the fake never gets a DB echo so it sits on screen at seq=0 forever, (c) fire 'cleared' to blank the victim's chat view, (d) fire 'mood' with an arbitrary gif URL that the victim's app loads via Image.network. Separately: hard 300-message ceiling with no scroll-back pagination; O(n log n) full re-sort per message (catch-up of 500 rows = 500 setStates and 500 full sorts); _messages grows unbounded across catch-ups; ChatScreen is rendered directly in a Column in app_shell.dart L238-241, NOT an IndexedStack, so switching tabs DISPOSES the screen — all three chat channels are torn down and 300 rows are refetched on every return to the Chat tab.
modules.scale_reason: postgres_changes re-evaluates the messages RLS policy per change per connected subscriber, and the policy calls public.current_user_couple_id() unwrapped (not `(select ...)`), so it is re-evaluated per row rather than cached as an InitPlan. Every open chat holds 3 channels. The public broadcast topic is a confidentiality and integrity hole that scales linearly with user count — one leaked couple_id is a full live wiretap. The 300-row no-pagination fetch on every tab switch multiplies REST load by navigation frequency.

modules.name: chat.send.text
modules.purpose: Send a text message with instant on-screen feedback.
modules.tables: public.messages insert {id (client-generated uuid v4), couple_id, sender_id, body, kind:'text', reply_to_id}
modules.realtime_or_push: Fires broadcast 'msg' on mood_burst:<coupleId> FIRST, then awaits the Postgres insert. Both carry the same client-minted uuid so they dedupe.
modules.current_mechanism: Client mints a uuid v4, renders the bubble locally via _onIncoming, broadcasts it, then inserts to Postgres. The insert is wrapped in a bare `try { } catch (_) { /* it's already on screen */ }` — L125-129. There is NO retry, NO persistence, NO queue for text. If the insert fails (offline, RLS reject, socket up but REST down), the message stays on the sender's screen looking sent forever and never reaches the partner or the database. It is lost silently on app restart.
modules.known_weaknesses: Silent permanent data loss on any insert failure — the only send path in the module with no failure state at all (images get a retry button, text gets a swallowed exception). The bubble shows a single grey tick indistinguishable from a genuinely-sent message. Also: text is NOT routed through ChatSendQueue, so the queue's whole 'a send must survive the screen that started it' guarantee does not apply to the most common message type.
modules.scale_reason: On flaky mobile networks at population scale this is a steady background rate of vanished messages with zero telemetry and zero user-visible signal — the classic 'she never texted me' failure the repo's own message_push.sql comment describes, reintroduced on the write side.

modules.name: chat.send.media (image / video / voice / GIF) + optimistic send queue
modules.purpose: Upload media to Storage and insert the corresponding message row without making the user watch the upload.
modules.entry_points: E:/LDR/mobile/lib/features/chat/chat_send_queue.dart (whole file); chat_repository.dart sendImage L241-258, sendVideo L271-286, sendVoice L301-316, uploadGif L262-267, signedVideoUrl L289-298; chat_screen.dart _sendImageFast L230-234, _adoptPending L241-279, _attachGif L200-221, _flingGifFile L189-196; chat_input_bar.dart L95-177; E:/LDR/mobile/lib/features/chat/rapid_camera_screen.dart _send L508-541; E:/LDR/mobile/lib/core/services/photo_picker_service.dart
modules.tables: public.messages (image_path / voice_path / video_path + kind). Storage buckets: 'couple_media' (PUBLIC — images and voice notes, served via getPublicUrl, path <coupleId>/<img|voice|gif>_<epochMs><12 hex>.<ext>), 'couple_intimate' (PRIVATE — videos, served via createSignedUrl 3600s), 'chat-bg' (PUBLIC — chat background images, path <uid>/bg_<epochMs>.jpg). NONE of these three buckets or their storage.objects policies exist in E:/LDR/supabase/*.sql — only 'capsule-media' is created in SQL (capsules.sql L110-119). They are dashboard-configured, undocumented, unreproducible.
modules.realtime_or_push: Images: after upload, ChatSendQueue calls ChatBroadcastService.broadcastImage — but only if ChatBroadcastService.active is non-null, i.e. only if ChatScreen is currently mounted. Video, voice and everything else rely solely on the postgres_changes INSERT echo. Plus the FCM push trigger on every insert.
modules.current_mechanism: ChatSendQueue is a ChangeNotifier singleton holding a plain in-memory List<PendingSend>. enqueueImage/enqueueVideo return immediately and run the upload with unawaited(). ChatScreen mirrors the queue into _messages via _adoptPending (listener + on mount), rendering the local File instantly with sendStatus=sending. On success the queue removes the entry and the DB echo reconciles the bubble by id; on failure the entry is kept as failed and the bubble grows a Retry chip (chat_screen.dart L1644-1675). Images pass through PhotoPickerService: crop → resize to max 1200px → JPEG q80 before upload. GIFs take two different paths: 'Fling a GIF' uploads to couple_media and broadcasts a mood-burst URL with NO message row at all (ephemeral, lost on both phones after ~5.2s); 'Attach GIF' HTTP-GETs the GIPHY URL to a temp file and sends it as a normal image message. Keyboard-inserted GIFs (Gboard) go to the fling path.
modules.known_weaknesses: CONFIRMED BUG — video duplicates for the sender: ChatSendQueue._enqueue passes id=null for video (chat_send_queue.dart L62-63) and ChatRepository.sendVideo inserts WITHOUT an id (chat_repository.dart L279-285), so Postgres assigns gen_random_uuid(). The optimistic bubble's uuid never matches the DB row, _onIncoming treats the echo as a new message, and the sender ends up with two bubbles — one dead (videoPath null, tap does nothing, _VideoBubble L1921) and one real. Images do not have this bug (id is threaded through). TWO DIFFERENT VIDEO PATHS: the input bar's attach sheet calls ChatRepository.sendVideo directly (blocking, no optimistic bubble, no queue, no retry — chat_screen.dart L1208-1209), while the rapid camera uses the queue. Voice notes likewise bypass the queue entirely (blocking upload, spinner in the input bar, no retry). On 404/UNREGISTERED/NOT_FOUND it nulls the recipient's fcm_token; it always returns 200 so pg_net never retry-storms. modules.scale_reason: This is the hard ceiling. Every chat message triggers one synchronous pg_net enqueue plus one edge-function invocation that performs an RSA signature and a Google OAuth exchange before sending — per message, per couple, with no token cache, no batching, and no suppression for online recipients. At thousands of users chatting this is edge-function invocations and Google token-endpoint calls scaling linearly with total message volume, and pg_net's single fire-and-forget queue plus an unbounded net._http_response table sits directly in the write path of the busiest table in the app.

NOT a private channel — no `RealtimeChannelConfig(private: true)` anywhere, and no `realtime.messages` RLS policy exists in any file under E:/LDR/supabase/*.sql. The topic is joinable by anyone holding the anon key and a couple UUID. Echo suppression is application-level only: `if (payload['from'] == _myUid) return`, where `_myUid = session.profile?.id` is captured once in `init()` (:431) and never refreshed. Re-subscribe is Pattern A (await `removeChannel(old)`, then re-create) guarded by `_subscribingChan`. modules.scale_reason: The topic is an unauthenticated, guessable-by-UUID public broadcast room; call teardown and call injection are available to anyone who can enumerate or obtain a couple id. Beyond security, the design needs both apps foregrounded and unlocked-past-the-cover with a live websocket to work at all — the realtime path is best-effort at every hop, and the couple-scoped topic means no multi-device story exists.
